new_points.title: Pope Leo’s recovery from lung cancer surgery ‘progressing as planned’

new_points.title: Mont Blanc, the ‘roof of Europe’, loses more than a metre of height in a year
new_points.content: Peak of French mountain now 4,807 metres high and fluctuates year by year due to changes in Alpine climateEurope’s highest mountain shrank by more than a metre last year. The peak of Mont Blanc in France now stands 4,807.47 metres above sea level, a team of surveyors said on Wednesday, putting “the roof of Europe” 1.29 metres lower than in 2025.The mountain is about 4,792 metres tall but the summit constantly shifts as heat, wind and precipitation change the thickness of snow and ice on top. The height scientists recorded during an expedition last month was 1.88 metres greater than it was in 2023, when it reached the lowest levels in recent memory.

new_points.title: Container ship sinks near strait of Hormuz amid surge in Iranian attacks

new_points.title: US inflation rose to 3.7% in September in blow to Republicans before midterms

This final inflation report before the pivotal midterm elections comes amid polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with the Trump administration over the cost of living.

new_points.title: Ken Paxton stirs vaccine skepticism to ingratiate himself with Maha movement

Paxton linked his efforts to a campaign against vaccines from Donald Trump and Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and directly referenced the Maha movement in his announcement. The president endorsed Paxton’s Senate run in May.

new_points.title: How we lost our appetite for eat-the-rich satire

new_points.title: Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
new_points.content: For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimer’s disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.

new_points.title: The secret to easier exercise as an adult may start in childhood
new_points.content: Exercise during childhood could have a surprising lifelong benefit, potentially making physical activity less exhausting in adulthood. In a study involving guinea fowl, researchers discovered that birds accustomed to carrying weights while growing up could carry those weights as adults without using extra energy, while untrained birds burned 23% more.

new_points.title: Scientists reveal why some workout recovery tricks can backfire
new_points.content: Ice baths, massages, compression garments, and recovery supplements promise faster muscle recovery, but research suggests their benefits are often overstated, and some techniques may even undermine long-term gains. Scientists say the most effective recovery methods are far simpler and cheaper: getting enough sleep, eating well, and giving muscles time to rebuild.

new_points.title: Cornell scientists identify rare human genetic disorder in two unusually long-legged cats
new_points.content: Two unusually long-legged cats have helped scientists uncover the first genetically confirmed cases of Marfan syndrome in domestic felines. Researchers at Cornell University discovered that the brothers carried two altered copies of a gene linked to the rare connective tissue disorder, which can affect the eyes, heart, and blood vessels. Surprisingly, the cats survived into adulthood because their genetic mutation still allowed some normal function.

new_points.title: Scientists discover how harmful “zombie cells” hide from the immune system

new_points.title: Scientists may have finally solved the mystery of the Moon’s two faces
